Good news — I found current info on Claude Cowork. Here's what you need to know before diving into your project:

What Claude Cowork Actually Is

Claude Cowork is Anthropic's tool for letting non-developers delegate tasks and workflows to a Claude-based agent. It's now generally available on all paid Claude plans (Pro, Team, Enterprise). It's designed to transform Claude from a conversational chatbot into an active participant in your desktop workflow, allowing it to manage files and execute multi-step tasks autonomously — with a simplified graphical interface tailored for non-technical users and general administrative tasks.

So Cowork is a desktop agentic tool — it's separate from this chat interface. It can work with files on your computer, connect to apps like Google Drive, and run multi-step tasks with your approval at key steps.

For Your Course Transformation Project

Your idea is a great fit for an AI-assisted workflow, but I want to set accurate expectations:

What Cowork could do: Open your files (syllabus, slides, assignments), pass content to Claude, and save outputs (lesson plans, markdown notes, instructor guides) back to your filesystem — without you manually copy-pasting.

What this chat interface can do right now: The same thing, just with you uploading files directly here. I can read your syllabus, analyze slide content or transcripts, and produce all the deliverables you listed — detailed lesson plans, markdown lecture notes, assignments + instructor guidance — in a structured, reverse-classroom format.

My Recommendation

Rather than waiting to set up Cowork, we can start right here with the same results. The workflow would be:

You share the syllabus first → I'll map out the full reverse-classroom structure

You provide slides/transcripts lesson by lesson → I generate markdown notes + pre-class materials

You share existing assignments → I redesign them with instructor guidance

Want to start by uploading your syllabus? That'll let me propose a full lesson plan framework tailored to your R & Statistics course before we touch anything else.

Here's your full course mapped out. A few things worth flagging before we start producing materials:

What I noticed from the syllabus

Strengths for the flip. The 8-week structure is clean, and the progression is logical — each week builds on the last. Weeks 1–2 (R mechanics) are excellent candidates for pre-recorded walkthroughs, since students can pause, rewind, and practice at their own pace. Weeks 3–5 (stats + modeling) are where in-class time becomes most valuable, since interpreting results is where confusion clusters.

Week 6 (Survival Analysis) is the most technically dense single-week topic and will need especially strong pre-class scaffolding — Kaplan-Meier and censoring are genuinely tricky conceptually.

Week 7 is already a flipped structure — project work time in class is exactly the right model. The pre-class piece I'd add is a structured draft template or outline so students come in with something rather than a blank page.

What I'll produce for you, week by week

Markdown lecture notes
Student-facing content distilled from your slides/recordings — readable as a standalone reference
Assignment + instructor guide
Revised assignment with clear instructions, rubric, sample answers, and facilitation tips

Ready to start

The most efficient path is to go week by week, using your existing slides or recording transcripts as the source material. You can share them in any order.

To kick things off: drop the Week 1 materials (slides and/or a transcript) and I'll generate the full Week 1 package — lesson plan, markdown notes, and assignment with instructor guide — as a set of downloadable files.
Before that, can we create a lesson plan where videos are optional. Many students prefer reading over watching video.

Absolutely — that's a pedagogically sound choice, and it removes a barrier for students who learn better through text. The pre-class materials will be reading-first, with videos listed as optional enrichment for those who want them.

Here's how the pre-class structure would look for each week:

Primary (required): Markdown reading notes + a short comprehension check (quiz or reflection prompt)
Optional: Video walkthrough of the same material (for students who want to see it demonstrated)

This also makes your job easier — the markdown notes I generate are the primary pre-class material, not just a supplement to a video you'd have to record separately.

A few other questions to nail down the lesson plan template before I start building it:

How long are your class sessions? (e.g., 60 min, 90 min) — this affects how I structure the in-class activity flow and timing

Group size? Knowing whether "pair work" means 2 students or 4–5 helps calibrate the activities

Any tools already in use? (e.g., RStudio Cloud / Posit Cloud, a course LMS, Google Colab) — I'll reference whichever environment students will actually be working in
Classes are 90 minutes

Got it. For group size and tools, I'll make reasonable assumptions — small groups of 3–4 (typical for a cohort-style program like PROPEL) and Posit Cloud since it removes the local install barrier. You can correct either if needed.

Great idea — markdown files on GitHub (or a GitHub Wiki) are perfect for this. Students can access them from any browser, and you can update them without redistributing files.

Before I start writing, a few quick questions to make sure the content and structure are right:

Take your time — your answers here will shape the structure for all the markdown content.

Q: What should the markdown lessons include? (Select all that apply)
A: Narrative explanations of concepts, Code examples with comments, Knowledge check questions (from slides), Exercises / practice problems, Links to optional videos

Q: How should lessons and assignments be organized?
A: Lessons and assignments in separate folders

Q: For code blocks, which dataset should exercises use by default?
A: Palmer Penguins (built into R, no download needed)

Perfect. One more thing before I start — GitHub repos and wikis have slightly different tradeoffs for this use case:

GitHub Repository — files live in folders, students can see the full structure at a glance, and you can organize it exactly as planned (lessons/, assignments/). Easier to maintain and link to specific files.

GitHub Wiki — cleaner reading experience, built-in sidebar navigation, but less flexible folder structure and harder to bulk-edit.

For a course with this many files (likely 20+ lesson files + assignment files), a repository with a clear folder structure and a README as the course homepage will be much easier to manage. I'd recommend that unless you have a strong preference for the wiki.

How can I save this entire conversation for reference/transparency?

A few good options depending on what you want to do with it:

Easiest — Claude.ai built-in export
Go to the conversation in the sidebar → click the three-dot menu (⋯) next to the conversation title → "Export conversation." Claude.ai can export as a text or JSON file you can save locally.

Browser — save as PDF
Open this conversation in your browser, then File → Print → Save as PDF. This preserves the formatted layout including code blocks, which is useful if you want a readable document to share with colleagues or attach to a grant.

Copy to a document
Select all (Ctrl/Cmd+A on the page), paste into a Word doc or Google Doc. Less clean than PDF but editable — useful if you want to annotate decisions you made along the way.

For transparency specifically — if you're documenting AI use for a research or institutional context, the JSON export is the most complete record since it includes timestamps and the full exchange. The PDF is better for human readers. You could also drop a note in your GitHub repo's README (e.g., "Course materials developed with Claude Sonnet 4.6 — conversation log available on request") and attach the export.

Is there a specific context you're documenting this for — institutional, research, just personal records? That might affect which format makes the most sense.

Apologies for the bad info earlier. Here's what actually works:

Official full account export
Click your initials in the lower-left corner of Claude → Settings → there's a built-in export option. This exports your entire conversation history and sends you a .dms file, which is a renamed ZIP archive. This is the most complete official method, but it exports all conversations, not just this one.

Save as PDF (simplest for a single conversation)
With the conversation open, press Ctrl+P (Windows) or Cmd+P (Mac), then in print options choose "Save as PDF." This is the fastest option for just this conversation.

Browser extension (most flexible)
The "AI Chat Exporter" Chrome extension lets you save conversations as PDF, Markdown, Text, CSV, or JSON with a couple of clicks. Your conversations never leave your device — the extension operates entirely within your browser. It's a third-party tool, not affiliated with Anthropic, but widely used.

Manual copy
Select all with Ctrl+A (Windows) or Cmd+A (Mac), then copy and paste into a Word doc or Google Doc. Low-tech but always works.

For your transparency/reference use case, I'd suggest Save as PDF for a readable record you can share, plus the full account export from Settings if you want a structured data backup. The Chrome extension is handy if you find yourself doing this regularly.
